clinicalPearls: Brief episodes of rapid shivering or shuddering of the head, shoulders and trunk, as if experiencing a cold chill
Consciousness is fully preserved and there is no postictal drowsiness, distinguishing episodes from seizures
Attacks are very short, may occur many times a day and often happen during excitement, feeding or frustration
Onset is usually in infancy or early childhood and the episodes are benign and self-limiting
The electroencephalogram is normal, both during and between episodes
A possible association with later essential tremor has been suggested, and a family history of tremor may be present
reference.pathophysiology: Shuddering attacks are a benign non-epileptic paroxysmal event of early childhood, characterised by brief tremulous shivering movements with retained awareness. The mechanism is not fully understood but the movements resemble an exaggerated shiver, and the reported association with a family history of essential tremor has led to the hypothesis that they may be an early manifestation of a tremor tendency. There is no underlying structural or epileptic disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Gratification behaviour or other benign paroxysmal events
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the characteristic brief shivering with preserved awareness
Home video of episodes to support the diagnosis
Electroencephalogram only if seizures cannot be excluded clinically
Developmental and neurological assessment confirming normal findings
redFlags: Loss of awareness or postictal features suggesting seizures
Change in the pattern or emergence of new event types
reference.prognosis: The attacks are entirely benign and typically resolve during early childhood without treatment; development and later neurological health are normal.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing shuddering as epileptic seizures and starting unnecessary treatment
Ordering extensive investigation for a clearly benign event
Overlooking a family history of tremor
Failing to reassess if awareness is lost or the pattern changes
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Parental reassurance and education that the episodes are benign, self-limiting and require no drug treatment
Confirmation of the benign diagnosis clinically and with a home video of typical episodes, avoiding unnecessary investigation or antiepileptic medication
Electroencephalography reserved only for cases where seizures cannot be excluded clinically
Watchful monitoring of neurodevelopmental progress, with re-review if the episodes change in character
Advice on the recognised possible association with later essential tremor and note of any family history of tremor
Re-referral to paediatric neurology if awareness is lost during episodes, the events evolve, or development regresses
